issues.legal_issue: A consumer forum may award reasonable compensation beyond the amount fixed in a flat-purchase agreement when a developer’s substantial delay in handing over possession results from a breach of contract and the agreed compensation is inadequate under an unfair, one-sided bargain.
material_facts: The developer agreed to endeavour to complete the apartments within the contractual period, subject to specified exceptions, but possession was delayed by approximately two to four years.
The developer acknowledged the delay and had credited agreed delay compensation to many purchasers; no force majeure or other contractual exception explained the delay.
The agreement imposed substantially harsher consequences for late payment by purchasers than for late delivery by the developer.
Purchasers had paid a substantial part of the price and faced continuing financial and personal hardship while awaiting possession.
issues.conclusion: The agreed monthly compensation did not limit the consumer forum’s power to award just and reasonable compensation. The purchasers, apart from those who had entered specific settlements or transferred their interests, were awarded simple interest on the amounts paid from the expiry of the contractual completion period until the offer of possession after receipt of the occupancy certificate, in addition to compensation already credited under the agreement.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(1)(g), 2(1)(o) and 14(1)(e) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, failure to provide contracted housing services within the agreed period is a deficiency, and the consumer forum may direct its removal and award restitutionary compensation. Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta and Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Balbir Singh recognize compensation for consumer loss, harassment and suffering; Balbir Singh requires compensation to be related to loss or injury without prescribing a rigid formula. R.V. Prasannakumaar v. Mantri Castles and Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Govindan Raghavan recognize that an inadequate, one-sided contractual remedy need not constrain an award of just compensation. DLF Homes Panchkula Pvt. Ltd. v. D.S. Dhanda does not impose an absolute bar on compensation beyond the agreed rate: it rejects arbitrary awards lacking a connection to the default and requires strong reasons to depart from the contractual rate. Here, the substantial delay, inadequate agreed recompense, and imbalance in the agreement supplied those reasons.

rule.if: consumer_complaint_appeal and housing_service_dispute and admitted_possession_delay and substantial_delay and one_sided_agreement and inadequate_contractual_recompense and not applicable_delay_exception

predicates.consumer_complaint_appeal: The buyers pursued an appeal arising from a consumer complaint about housing services.
predicates.housing_service_dispute: The dispute concerned a developer’s performance of its undertaking to provide completed homes to buyers.
predicates.admitted_possession_delay: The developer acknowledged that it had not delivered possession within the expected contractual period.
predicates.substantial_delay: The delay in delivering possession extended materially beyond the contractual completion period.
predicates.one_sided_agreement: The agreement imposed materially harsher consequences on buyers for default than on the developer for delayed delivery.
predicates.inadequate_contractual_recompense: The compensation fixed in the agreement did not reasonably recompense buyers for the consequences of the delay.
predicates.applicable_delay_exception: A contractual exception, such as a force majeure circumstance, accounted for the developer’s failure to deliver on time.

issues.definition: When buyers bring a consumer appeal about housing services and the developer admits a substantial delay that is not explained by an applicable exception, a one-sided agreement with inadequate delay compensation does not prevent an award of reasonable compensation beyond that payment.

issues.legal_issue: Taking possession of a home or executing its conveyance does not, by itself, extinguish a buyer’s consumer claim for compensation for delayed possession.
material_facts: The developer informed buyers that it would not deliver possession or execute conveyance documents if buyers reserved their rights or accepted possession under protest.
Buyers were therefore presented with a choice between pursuing their claims and obtaining possession or perfecting title to the homes for which they had paid.
The underlying transaction included the developer’s undertaking to construct homes and provide associated services and amenities.
issues.conclusion: Buyers who obtained possession or executed conveyance deeds did not thereby lose their right to claim compensation for delayed possession. The transaction remained one involving housing services and was not converted into a mere sale of immovable property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(1)(o) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 includes housing construction and related facilities within the meaning of service. Narne Construction (P) Ltd. v. Union of India distinguishes a simple transfer of immovable property from a transaction in which a developer undertakes to provide development and facilities; a deficiency in the latter remains actionable before a consumer forum. It would be unreasonable to require a purchaser to indefinitely defer obtaining title or to surrender a claim as the price of obtaining a conveyance.

rule.if: consumer_complaint_appeal and developer_housing_service_undertaking and delayed_possession_claim and conveyance_or_possession_required_to_secure_home and protest_or_claim_reservation_refused

predicates.consumer_complaint_appeal: The buyer pursued an appeal arising from a consumer complaint about a housing transaction.
predicates.developer_housing_service_undertaking: The developer undertook to construct homes or provide related facilities rather than merely transfer property on an as-is basis.
predicates.delayed_possession_claim: The buyer sought compensation for the developer’s delay in delivering possession.
predicates.conveyance_or_possession_required_to_sec: The buyer needed possession or conveyance to obtain the home or perfect title to it.
predicates.protest_or_claim_reservation_refused: The developer refused to allow possession or conveyance while the buyer reserved a claim or recorded a protest.

issues.definition: When a developer undertakes housing services and refuses to permit a buyer to secure the home while reserving a delayed-possession claim, obtaining possession or conveyance does not bar that claim.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who entered a specific settlement with the developer is excluded from the compensation awarded to other purchasers when no specific evidence establishes coercion or undue influence.
material_facts: Eleven purchasers entered specific settlement deeds with the developer.
The purchasers did not produce specific material demonstrating that the settlement deeds were executed under coercion or undue influence.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers who entered the specific settlement deeds were excluded from the compensation order and held to the terms of their settlements.
issues.legal_principle: A purchaser who enters a specific settlement is held to its terms where the record contains no specific material establishing coercion or undue influence. The judgment applies the terms of the settlement bargain and the requirement that a claim of coercion or undue influence be supported by evidence; it cites no statutory provision or earlier case for this determination.

predicates.consumer_complaint_appeal: The purchaser’s claim arose in an appeal concerning a consumer complaint.
predicates.specific_settlement_executed: The purchaser entered a specific settlement with the developer.
predicates.no_specific_coercion_evidence: The purchaser produced no specific evidence that the settlement was obtained through coercion or undue influence.

issues.definition: A purchaser who settled a consumer dispute is excluded from the compensation order when the purchaser produces no specific evidence that the settlement was coerced or improperly induced.

issues.legal_issue: An original purchaser who transfers the home and a later purchaser who acquires it with knowledge of the existing delay are not entitled to the compensation awarded for the original purchaser’s delay-related hardship.
material_facts: Three purchasers transferred their interests in their apartments to third parties.
The later purchasers acquired the interests knowing that delivery had been delayed.
The later purchasers did not experience hardship comparable to that suffered by the original purchasers who had waited for delivery.
issues.conclusion: The purchasers who transferred their interests were excluded from the benefit of the compensation order, and later purchasers could not claim that benefit by stepping into the original purchasers’ shoes.
issues.legal_principle: HUDA v. Raje Ram distinguishes original allottees who endured delay from later transferees who acquired their interests with knowledge of the delay. The latter cannot claim compensation for the original purchasers’ mental agony and hardship where they did not experience comparable injury.

rule.if: consumer_complaint_appeal and original_buyer_transferred_interest and later_buyer_knew_of_delay and no_comparable_delay_hardship

predicates.consumer_complaint_appeal: The claim arose in an appeal concerning a consumer complaint about delayed home delivery.
predicates.original_buyer_transferred_interest: An original buyer transferred the buyer’s interest in the home to another person.
predicates.later_buyer_knew_of_delay: The later buyer acquired the interest knowing that delivery had been delayed.
predicates.no_comparable_delay_hardship: The later buyer did not suffer hardship comparable to the original buyer’s experience of waiting for delivery.

issues.definition: An original buyer who transfers the home and a later buyer who knowingly acquires it without comparable delay-related hardship are not entitled to the compensation awarded for the original buyer’s delay.

issues.legal_issue: A developer does not commit a deficiency in providing a promised clubhouse when it has constructed the clubhouse and its associated facilities, even though transfer of management to the residents’ association remains pending.
material_facts: The developer constructed a clubhouse with the promised associated facilities.
An occupancy certificate had been received for the clubhouse.
The developer’s account of construction and the status of handover was not disputed by the purchasers.
issues.conclusion: There was no breach of the developer’s obligation to provide a constructed clubhouse facility.
issues.legal_principle: A deficiency under Section 2(1)(g) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 requires a fault, shortcoming or inadequacy in the performance undertaken. On the facts, construction of the clubhouse and receipt of its occupancy certificate established performance of the obligation to provide the constructed facility; the court relied on no earlier case for this issue.

rule.if: consumer_complaint_appeal and clubhouse_promised and clubhouse_constructed and occupancy_approval_received

predicates.consumer_complaint_appeal: The purchasers raised the clubhouse claim in an appeal arising from a consumer complaint.
predicates.clubhouse_promised: The developer represented that a clubhouse would be provided to purchasers.
predicates.clubhouse_constructed: The developer completed construction of the clubhouse and its associated facilities.
predicates.occupancy_approval_received: The competent authority issued an occupancy certificate for the clubhouse.

issues.definition: When a promised clubhouse has been constructed and has received occupancy approval, the developer has not failed to provide the constructed facility merely because management handover remains pending.

issues.legal_issue: A developer’s failure to provide amenities clearly represented as part of the residential development is a deficiency even when purchasers have no property interest in the land on which those amenities were to be built and similar facilities later become available nearby.
material_facts: The developer’s brochure represented that the wider township would include a shopping centre, an early-learning school and healthcare facilities.
Purchasers booked homes in reliance on representations about the development and its amenities.
The agreement excluded purchasers’ title or interest in land and facilities outside their residential complex, but the developer had not provided the represented wider-township amenities.
The developer argued that similar facilities had since become available in the surrounding area.
issues.conclusion: The developer was accountable for its failure to provide the clearly represented amenities; the availability of other facilities nearby did not cure that failure. The purchasers were entitled to compensation for the unfulfilled representations.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(1)(g) of the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 treats a shortcoming in the quality, nature or manner of performance undertaken in relation to a service as a deficiency. A lack of title or interest in external facilities does not excuse failure to perform a clear representation that induced purchasers to invest. Developers remain accountable for representations about the amenities they will provide, and later availability of alternative facilities does not discharge that obligation.

rule.if: consumer_complaint_appeal and clear_amenity_representation and buyer_reliance and promised_amenities_not_provided and alternative_nearby_facilities_only

predicates.consumer_complaint_appeal: The purchasers raised the amenity claim in an appeal arising from a consumer complaint.
predicates.clear_amenity_representation: The developer clearly represented that specified amenities would be provided as part of the development.
predicates.buyer_reliance: The purchasers invested in the homes in response to the developer’s representations about the development.
predicates.promised_amenities_not_provided: The developer failed to provide amenities it had represented would be provided.
predicates.alternative_nearby_facilities_only: The developer relied on similar facilities that became available elsewhere in the surrounding area rather than providing the promised amenities.

issues.definition: When buyers rely on clear representations about development amenities and those amenities are not provided, alternative facilities nearby do not remove the developer’s liability for deficiency and compensation.

issues.legal_issue: A developer may recover from purchasers their proportionate share of tax interest where the agreement allocates the tax burden to purchasers and the developer explains that the timing of liability was uncertain; the developer may not pass on a penalty it did not charge to purchasers.
material_facts: The agreement required purchasers to bear a proportionate share of taxes connected with construction and the development.
The developer explained that the liability for the relevant construction tax was unclear while related litigation was pending and that the issue was later settled by a court decision.
The developer passed on the interest component on a proportionate basis but did not pass on the penalty.
issues.conclusion: The demand for the purchasers’ proportionate share of interest on the tax did not constitute a deficiency of service.
issues.legal_principle: The express tax-allocation terms in the agreement governed the purchasers’ proportionate liability. Larsen and Toubro Ltd. v. State of Karnataka resolved the relevant uncertainty about construction tax. In light of those contractual terms and the explanation for the timing of payment, the court found no deficiency in passing on the tax interest; it noted that no penalty had been passed on.

predicates.consumer_complaint_appeal: The purchasers challenged the tax-related demand in an appeal arising from a consumer complaint.
predicates.agreement_allocates_proportionate_tax_bu: The agreement requires purchasers to bear a proportionate share of taxes connected with the development.
predicates.tax_liability_timing_was_uncertain: The timing of the relevant tax liability was uncertain while its legal treatment was being resolved.
predicates.developer_passed_on_interest_but_not_pen: The developer charged purchasers a proportionate share of tax interest but did not charge them the tax penalty.

issues.definition: A proportionate tax-interest demand is not a service deficiency when the agreement allocates the tax burden, the timing of liability was uncertain, and the developer did not pass on a penalty.

issues.legal_issue: A developer may recover purchasers’ proportionate share of the cost of electricity infrastructure when the agreement authorizes recovery and the infrastructure was required to supply the development.
material_facts: The agreement authorized recovery from purchasers of their proportionate share of costs for electricity-supply infrastructure.
The electricity supplier required a dedicated substation as the project’s electricity needs increased.
The developer constructed the substation and sought to recover its cost proportionately from purchasers.
issues.conclusion: The electricity-infrastructure charges were consistent with the agreement, and the consumer commission’s decision upholding them was not infirm.
issues.legal_principle: The agreement expressly provided for purchasers to pay their proportionate share of payments and infrastructure costs associated with bulk electricity supply. The court found the charges consistent with that contractual term and relied on no earlier case in reaching its conclusion.

rule.if: consumer_complaint_appeal and agreement_authorizes_proportionate_electricity_infrastructure_costs and dedicated_infrastructure_required and developer_incurred_infrastructure_cost

predicates.consumer_complaint_appeal: The purchasers challenged electricity charges in an appeal arising from a consumer complaint.
predicates.agreement_authorizes_proportionate_elect: The agreement permits the developer to recover purchasers’ proportionate share of electricity-infrastructure costs.
predicates.dedicated_infrastructure_required: The electricity supplier required dedicated infrastructure to provide electricity to the development.
predicates.developer_incurred_infrastructure_cost: The developer constructed the required infrastructure and incurred its cost.

issues.definition: When the agreement authorizes proportional recovery, required electricity infrastructure has been constructed, and the developer incurred its cost, proportional infrastructure charges are permitted.

issues.legal_issue: A developer may charge purchasers separately for the exclusive use of earmarked parking spaces when the charges are disclosed and included as a separate part of the agreed apartment price.
material_facts: The agreement separately included parking charges in the breakdown of the apartment price and distinguished parking from the price calculated by super area.
The brochure disclosed the parking charges to purchasers.
The purchasers relied on a statutory argument treating parking areas as common areas, but the court found the demand consistent with the agreement.
issues.conclusion: The parking charges were payable under the agreement and did not constitute a deficiency of service.
issues.legal_principle: The agreement separately provided for parking charges for exclusive use of earmarked spaces, and the charges were disclosed to purchasers. Nahalchand Laloochand Pvt. Ltd. v. Panchali Cooperative Housing Society Ltd. turned on Maharashtra legislation and was explained in DLF Ltd. v. Manmohan Lowe; the court distinguished that statutory context and concluded that the demand under this agreement did not establish a deficiency.

rule.if: consumer_complaint_appeal and parking_for_exclusive_earmarked_use and separate_parking_charge_disclosed and agreement_includes_separate_parking_charge

predicates.consumer_complaint_appeal: The purchasers challenged parking charges in an appeal arising from a consumer complaint.
predicates.parking_for_exclusive_earmarked_use: The charge concerned parking spaces earmarked for the exclusive use of purchasers.
predicates.separate_parking_charge_disclosed: The parking charge was disclosed to purchasers before or when they agreed to buy.
predicates.agreement_includes_separate_parking_char: The agreement separately included the parking charge in the breakdown of the apartment price.

issues.definition: When an agreement separately includes a disclosed charge for parking space earmarked for a purchaser’s exclusive use, the developer may collect that charge.
